title: Single units, multielectrode arrays, and Neuropixels
text:
CHAPTER 10. RECORDING THE LIVING BRAIN
SECTION 10.2. SINGLE UNITS, MULTIELECTRODE ARRAYS, AND NEUROPIXELS

The neuron's voice

EEG listens to the roar of a crowd. To understand computation, neuroscientists also want to hear individual voices: the spikes of single neurons, ideally many of them at once. This section traces the development of extracellular recording, from single nerve fibers in the 1920s to silicon probes that record from thousands of neurons simultaneously. It is a story of engineering, and it is still accelerating. For a mechatronics student, this is perhaps the most directly relevant area of neuroscience technology: microfabrication, low-noise analog electronics, wireless telemetry, and real-time signal processing all play central roles.

Adrian and the all-or-none code

In the 1920s, Edgar Adrian at Cambridge used a capillary electrometer and later vacuum tube amplifiers (which had become available through radio technology) to record electrical activity from single sensory nerve fibers. Working with Yngve Zotterman, he dissected a frog muscle until only one stretch receptor (muscle spindle) remained connected to its nerve fiber, and recorded the impulses as the muscle was stretched with different weights. He found three key facts:

1. Each impulse had the same size and shape, regardless of the strength of the stimulus (all-or-none).
2. Stronger stimuli produced a higher frequency of impulses (rate coding).
3. With a constant stimulus, the frequency gradually declined (adaptation).

Adrian summarized these findings in his book The Basis of Sensation (1928). He also connected the amplifier output to a loudspeaker so he could hear the impulses as clicks, a practice still used by electrophysiologists today, who often find it easier to recognize neurons by ear. Adrian's results established the basic principle of neural coding: information is carried by the timing and rate of identical spikes. He shared the 1932 Nobel Prize with Sherrington.

Microelectrodes and single units in the brain

Recording from single neurons inside the brain required fine electrodes. As described in section 8.2, David Hubel developed tungsten microelectrodes in the 1950s, insulated except at the tip; glass micropipettes filled with salt solution were also used. When the tip of such an electrode is placed close to a neuron (within roughly 50 to 100 micrometers), it picks up the extracellular voltage changes caused by the neuron's action potentials, typically 50 to a few hundred microvolts in amplitude. These recordings are called "single unit" recordings, since one assumes (after careful checking) that the recorded spikes come from one neuron.

Single-unit recording made possible most of the classic discoveries in systems neuroscience: receptive fields in visual cortex (Hubel and Wiesel), place cells (O'Keefe), reward prediction errors in dopamine neurons (Schultz), persistent activity in prefrontal cortex (Fuster, Goldman-Rakic), and many more. Edward Evarts at the US National Institutes of Health developed methods in the 1960s for recording single neurons in awake, behaving monkeys trained to perform tasks, which allowed researchers to relate neural activity directly to perception, decision, and movement. This "behaving monkey" approach became the dominant paradigm in primate systems neuroscience.

The physics of extracellular recording

What does an extracellular electrode actually measure? When a neuron fires, current flows into the cell at the active region (mainly sodium current at the soma and axon initial segment) and out of the cell at other regions. In the extracellular space, this produces a pattern of potential changes: a negative deflection near the site where current enters (the sink) and positive deflections where current exits (sources). An electrode close to the soma of a firing neuron typically records a brief negative-going spike lasting about 1 millisecond.

The extracellular potential at a distance r from a point current source I in a medium of conductivity sigma is

  phi = I / (4 * pi * sigma * r)

So the potential falls off with distance, and for a dipole-like arrangement of sources and sinks it falls off faster, roughly as 1/r^2 or steeper at larger distances. This is why an electrode can isolate the spikes of neurons within about 100 micrometers, and why spike amplitude is a clue to distance. Detailed models of extracellular potentials, combining neuron morphology with volume conductor theory, have been developed by Gaute Einevoll, Christof Koch, Gyorgy Buzsaki, and others.

The same electrode also picks up slower signals, the local field potential (LFP), obtained by low-pass filtering the raw signal (typically below a few hundred Hz). The LFP reflects mainly synaptic currents in a region around the electrode, from hundreds of micrometers to millimeters, and it is related to EEG but with much better spatial resolution. Spikes are obtained by high-pass filtering (typically above about 300 Hz) and detecting threshold crossings.

Spike sorting

An electrode usually picks up spikes from several neurons near its tip. To study individual neurons, the spikes must be assigned to their source neurons, a process called spike sorting. Spikes from different neurons tend to have different shapes and amplitudes, depending on the neurons' distance and orientation relative to the electrode. Spike sorting typically involves:

1. Filtering and detecting spikes (threshold crossings).
2. Extracting features of each spike waveform, such as amplitudes, widths, or principal components.
3. Clustering the spikes in feature space, with each cluster corresponding (ideally) to one neuron.
4. Checking cluster quality, for example by verifying that spikes in a cluster obey a refractory period (no two spikes within about 1 to 2 milliseconds), which would be violated if spikes from two neurons were mixed.

Spike sorting is a classic unsupervised machine learning problem, and it remains challenging. Errors include merging two neurons into one cluster, splitting one neuron into two, and missing spikes that overlap in time. Modern algorithms, such as Kilosort (developed by Marius Pachitariu and colleagues, first released around 2016), use template matching and GPU acceleration to sort spikes from hundreds of channels.

Tetrodes

A simple idea greatly improved spike sorting: record with several closely spaced electrodes at once. If four fine wires are twisted together, their tips are separated by tens of micrometers, and each neuron's spike appears with a different amplitude on each wire, depending on its position. This gives a four-dimensional "signature" that makes sorting much more reliable, much as stereo hearing helps localize sounds. Bruce McNaughton, John O'Keefe, and Carol Barnes introduced the "stereotrode" (two wires) in 1983, and Charles Gray and colleagues and Michael Recce and O'Keefe developed the "tetrode" (four wires) in the late 1980s and 1990s. Tetrodes became the standard for recording hippocampal place cells in freely moving rats, and they made it possible to record dozens of neurons simultaneously, which led to the discovery of replay (section 9.2), since replay can only be detected in the joint activity of many cells.

Multielectrode arrays

To record from more neurons, researchers built arrays of many electrodes.

- Microwire arrays: bundles or grids of fine insulated wires, used in many labs, including by Miguel Nicolelis, John Chapin, and colleagues in the 1990s for recording ensembles of neurons in rats and monkeys.
- The Utah array: developed by Richard Normann and colleagues at the University of Utah in the late 1980s and 1990s. It is a 4 by 4 millimeter silicon chip with a 10 by 10 grid of needle-like electrodes (typically 96 of them wired for recording), each about 1 to 1.5 millimeters long, with a platinum or iridium oxide tip. It is inserted into the cortex with a pneumatic device at high speed. The Utah array is the main implant used in human brain-computer interface research, including the BrainGate trials (chapter 14), and it has been implanted in a number of people with paralysis.
- Planar silicon probes ("Michigan probes"): developed by Kensall Wise and colleagues at the University of Michigan, starting in the 1970s and 1980s, using microfabrication techniques from the semiconductor industry. These are thin silicon shanks with multiple recording sites along their length, allowing recording at many depths along a single insertion track.
- Multielectrode arrays for cultures and slices: flat arrays of electrodes on glass or silicon, on which neurons or brain slices are placed. Used extensively for studying retina (for example, by Markus Meister, E. J. Chichilnisky, and colleagues, who recorded from hundreds of retinal ganglion cells at once) and cultured networks.

Neuropixels

A major leap came with Neuropixels probes. Developed through a collaboration led by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus, the Allen Institute for Brain Science, the Gatsby Charitable Foundation, and University College London, with fabrication by imec (a Belgian microelectronics research center), the first Neuropixels probes were described in a 2017 paper in Nature by James Jun, Nicholas Steinmetz, Joshua Siegle, Daniel Denman, and many others, with Timothy Harris as a leading figure.

A Neuropixels 1.0 probe is a single silicon shank about 10 millimeters long, 70 micrometers wide, and about 24 micrometers thick, with 960 recording sites densely arranged along it. Any 384 of these sites can be selected for simultaneous recording. Crucially, the probe uses CMOS technology to integrate amplifiers, filters, multiplexers, and analog-to-digital converters directly on the probe base, so that only a few wires are needed to carry digitized data from hundreds of channels. This integration, standard in the semiconductor industry but new to neuroscience, solved the bottleneck of connecting hundreds of tiny electrodes to external electronics.

With Neuropixels, researchers could record from hundreds of well-isolated neurons across multiple brain regions simultaneously in mice. In 2019, Nicholas Steinmetz, Peter Zatka-Haas, Matteo Carandini, and Kenneth Harris reported in Nature recordings from approximately 30,000 neurons across about 42 brain regions in mice performing a visual discrimination task (combining many recording sessions), revealing how activity related to vision, choice, and action was distributed across the brain. Neuropixels 2.0, described in 2021 by Steinmetz and colleagues, used four shanks with 5,120 total sites and a smaller, lighter design suitable for long-term recordings in freely moving mice. Versions for primates (longer probes) and for humans (used in short intraoperative recordings) have also been developed; in 2022, teams including Angelique Paulk, Sydney Cash, and colleagues, and Ziv Williams and colleagues, reported Neuropixels recordings from human cortex during neurosurgery.

Large-scale and open data

High-density recording has changed how systems neuroscience is done. Instead of recording one neuron at a time and building up a picture over months, researchers now record from hundreds or thousands of neurons in a single session, observing how populations of neurons work together. This has driven several trends:

- Population analysis. Researchers analyze the joint activity of many neurons as a trajectory in a high-dimensional state space, using dimensionality reduction methods (chapter 13). For example, Mark Churchland, Krishna Shenoy, and colleagues showed in 2012 that the population activity of motor cortex during reaching shows rotational dynamics, which they interpreted in terms of a dynamical system generating the movement.
- Brain-wide recordings. Large collaborative projects, such as the International Brain Laboratory (a consortium founded around 2017 to study decision-making in mice with standardized experiments across many labs) and the Allen Brain Observatory, record from many brain regions under standardized conditions and release the data openly. The International Brain Laboratory released a "brain-wide map" of neural activity during decision making from hundreds of thousands of neurons recorded with Neuropixels probes.
- Data standards. Formats such as Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) and archives such as the DANDI archive have been developed to share neurophysiology data.

Chronic implants and the biological response

For brain-computer interfaces and long-term studies, electrodes must remain in the brain for months or years. This is difficult. The brain reacts to an implanted electrode as a foreign body: microglia and astrocytes accumulate around it, forming a glial scar that can push neurons away and electrically insulate the electrode, and micromotion of the electrode relative to the soft brain tissue causes ongoing damage. Recording quality often declines over months. Approaches to improve longevity include smaller and more flexible electrodes (for example, polymer-based probes, "neural lace" or mesh electronics developed by Charles Lieber's group, and ultra-thin flexible threads like those used by the company Neuralink), coatings that reduce inflammation, and materials that better match the mechanical properties of brain tissue. This is a materials science and mechanical engineering problem as much as a biological one.

Bridge to AI: data, decoding, and the scale of observation

High-density recording connects to AI in several ways.

Machine learning for analysis. Spike sorting, behavioral tracking (using deep learning tools such as DeepLabCut, developed by Alexander Mathis, Mackenzie Mathis, and colleagues in 2018, which tracks animal body parts in video using transfer learning), and decoding of neural activity all rely on machine learning. Latent variable models, such as LFADS (Latent Factor Analysis via Dynamical Systems, developed by Chethan Pandarinath, David Sussillo, and colleagues, published in 2018), use recurrent neural networks to infer smooth underlying dynamics from noisy spike trains, and have improved decoding for brain-computer interfaces. Transformer-based models trained on large collections of neural recordings, sometimes called neural foundation models, are an emerging trend.

Comparison of scales. Neuropixels can record thousands of neurons; the mouse brain has around 70 million neurons, and the human brain about 86 billion. Even the largest recordings observe a tiny fraction. In contrast, in an artificial neural network, every unit and every weight can be observed exactly. This asymmetry has led some researchers to test neuroscience methods on artificial networks. A famous provocative study by Eric Jonas and Konrad Kording in 2017, "Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?", applied standard neuroscience analysis methods (lesions, tuning curves, correlations, dimensionality reduction) to a simulated classic microprocessor running video games, and found that the methods produced results that looked meaningful but did not reveal how the processor actually worked. The lesson is that more data alone is not enough; we also need good theories and the right analysis methods.

Neural data as AI training data. Some researchers have proposed using large-scale neural recordings to constrain or train AI models, for example by adding a loss term that encourages a network's internal representations to match neural data. Studies have reported that such "neural regularization" can make networks more robust, as with the V1-like front ends mentioned in section 8.3. This is a direct use of neuroscience data to improve AI.

Summary

- Adrian (1920s) recorded single sensory fibers, establishing all-or-none spikes, rate coding, and adaptation.
- Tungsten and glass microelectrodes enabled single-unit recording in the brain, including in awake behaving monkeys.
- Extracellular electrodes detect spikes from neurons within about 100 micrometers; local field potentials reflect synaptic currents in a broader region.
- Spike sorting assigns spikes to neurons, aided by tetrodes and modern algorithms such as Kilosort.
- Multielectrode arrays (microwires, the Utah array, Michigan probes) increased the number of simultaneously recorded neurons.
- Neuropixels probes (2017) integrate CMOS electronics on a thin shank with 960 sites and 384 channels, enabling recordings of hundreds to thousands of neurons across many brain regions.
- Chronic implants face biological reactions; flexible materials are being developed.
- Machine learning is essential for analyzing large-scale recordings; the "microprocessor" study warns that data without theory may mislead.
